title: All Animals in Bali You Should Know: The Local Guide
content:
Bali is often referred to as paradise on earth, rich in culture, nature, and wildlife in Bali. The island is home to many domestic species and wild animals in Bali, making it one of the world’s top destinations for honeymoon, solo travelers, or families alike.
From the forests to the villages, you’ll find a wide range of animals, from common spotted doves and monkeys to rare endemic species like the starling. This diversity shows how unique animals in this Earth’s paradise truly are, even though the island has no large predators like jaguars or tigers. This guide highlights some of the most well-known Bali animal species and includes safety tips for visitors.
Native Animals in Bali
Bali native animals are very diverse; some are nearly extinct, while others are exotic creatures that still live in the wild areas of forests. Balinese people love their animals, especially their pets and livestock, and they even create special offerings for God to bless them twice a year through the ceremony known as Tumpek Kandang. Here are the most popular animals:
Bali has many free-roaming dogs with short fur and upright ears, and you can easily find this type of bali animal everywhere on the island. One of the most recognized native dogs, the Kintamani dog, is thought to be one of the oldest dog breeds in the world.
This specific type of dog is also used in certain offerings, although it remains a cultural controversy. Dogs are an important part of Balinese life, but sadly, cases of poisoning and dog killings have occurred in the past. Since most dogs here are not vaccinated, visitors should avoid petting street dogs, as they can carry rabies.
Bali’s cats often live as semi-feral pets. That’s why most cats are not kept indoors and instead roam freely around villages. Many cats in this island have short or kinked tails due to local genetics, but they are generally shy.
These cats can sometimes be loud and may rummage through garbage cans in search of food. It’s recommended to keep garbage bins closed at night to avoid this. Cats in Bali are not always friendly and may carry illnesses, so it is best to avoid petting them.
3. Sapi Bali (Bali Cattle)
The Bali cattle, scientifically known as Bos javanicus domesticus, is a unique local cow breed. Unlike other cattle, animals like these were traditionally used to plow rice fields rather than for dairy farming. Some people breed them as livestock, and the price of a fully grown cow can reach IDR 20–30 million.
Because cows are sacred in Hindu culture, they are respected and well cared for. Most Balinese do not eat beef; instead, they breed and sell cattle mainly to the Muslim community living in Bali.
4. Monkey (Long-tailed Macaque):
The long-tailed macaque (Macaca fascicularis) is one of the most famous wild animals in Bali. In Hindu culture, this monkey has a deep connection with mythology, as it represents Hanoman, a loyal soldier of Shri Rama in the Ramayana epic.
The Bali monkeys live in places such as the Ubud Monkey Forest and temple areas like Pura Uluwatu, Pura Lempuyang, and Pura Pulaki. Monkeys are curious animal and sometimes steal food or items from visitors; if startled, one monkey may alert the entire group.
5. Chickens and Roosters
Free-range chickens are everywhere on this island, and many households raise chickens and roosters. Roosters crow loudly at dawn and throughout the day. In fact, the morning “cock-a-doodle-doo” is one of the most recognizable sounds of animals in Bali.
Traditionally, people here are raised roosters for eggs, meat, and cultural cockfights, but today they mostly serve as farm animals and natural alarm clocks. There is also a mystical story about chickens and roosters: if you see one wandering at night, locals believe it may not be real but instead a devil spirit taking the form of a chicken.
Several gecko species live in Bali, especially in houses, villages, and forested areas. The most famous is the Tokay gecko, a nocturnal Bali animal that makes a very loud “tok-kay” call at night.
These harmless lizards cling to walls and ceilings, feeding on insects, even mosquitoes, which is why many people in this island allow these animals to live in certain parts of their homes. In Balinese culture, Tokay geckos are often seen as symbols of good luck.
7. Monitor Lizards (Biawak)
Bali’s forests and rivers are home to water monitor lizards, locally known as biawak or alu. Their scientific name is Varanus salvator bivittatus, and they share the same genus as the Komodo dragon, an Indonesian endemic species that has survived since the age of dinosaurs.
These large reptiles can grow over 1 meter long but are generally shy and avoid people. They live near water like waterfalls in Ubud or jungle areas, and prey on fish, frogs, eggs, and chickens. While they look intimidating, monitor lizards rarely attack unless threatened, so they are not considered among the most dangerous animals in Bali.
8. Pigs (Wild Boars)
This paradise island also has wild pigs, or boars, that roam in its forests, especially in the western part of the island. These wild boars (Sus scrofa vittatus) are larger and have tusks compared to village pigs, and they are often seen in jungle areas or national parks.
Wild boars usually avoid humans, but they can charge if cornered, so it is best to keep a respectful distance. This type of pig is not commonly eaten by people here because the meat is muscular and tough, while the suckling pig (from village pigs) is the one traditionally enjoyed in Balinese cuisine.
9. Birds (Doves, Mynas, Bali Starling)
As of 2025, there are more than 300 bird species recognized in this island of God, making birds some of the most diverse animals in Bali. Common village birds include spotted doves and zebra doves, small gray-brown species often found in gardens.
Another familiar village bird is the pigeon, which has a green iridescent sheen on its neck. The Javan myna (white-vented myna), a black-and-white starling native to Bali and Java, is often seen living alongside buffalo, feeding on fleas found on their bodies.
Most famously, the endemic starling (also called Bali myna) is a bright white bird unique to the island. This Bali native animal is critically endangered in the wild, so it can only be seen in protected areas like West Bali National Park or in zoos.
There are many spider species in Bali, but almost all are harmless to humans. Visitors may encounter Golden Orbweavers, huntsman spiders, or grass spiders, which often live quietly around villages and houses. No serious cases of spider attacks have ever been reported in this island, reinforcing the fact that these creatures are not among the truly dangerous animals in Bali.
For example, the giant huntsman spider (Pantropical Huntsman) looks frightening due to its large size, but its bite is not dangerous to humans. Spiders here typically avoid contact with people and help by catching flies, mosquitoes, and other insects.
Bali is home to a variety of snakes, including some venomous species such as the King Cobra, Blue Krait, and Green Tree Pit Viper. These wild animals usually hide in tall grass or forested areas and often flee when they encounter people.
However, you should always be cautious, especially when walking through rice fields or forests where snakes may be present. Beaches and reefs are also home to sea snakes, which are highly venomous but typically shy.
If you encounter one, it’s best to remain calm and give it space; snakes generally do not attack unless provoked. Some temples here even consider sea snakes sacred, such as the holy cave sea snake at Tanah Lot Temple, which locals believe acts as a guardian spirit for the temple.
The tropical climate of Indonesia supports many butterfly species, making them some of the most colorful and charming Bali native animals. Villages that grow flowers for offerings naturally attract butterflies. Around 15 butterfly species are native to this paradise island, and one of the most popular is the Barong Butterfly, known for its unique colors and motifs.
The Bali Butterfly Park in Tabanan showcases all 15 native species along with many exotic butterflies from around the world. Visitors can enjoy the sight of butterflies fluttering around gardens, forests, and rice fields, adding to the richness of wildlife in Bali.
Sea turtles are a symbol of resilience and longevity in local beliefs. That’s why, when these Bali animals became endangered, conservation efforts were introduced to protect them. Today, many communities focus on preserving sea turtles through conservation centers and awareness programs.
Four species of sea turtles swim around the seas here: Hawksbill, Green, Loggerhead, and Olive Ridley turtles. These turtles occasionally nest on quiet beaches. Many local parks and dive centers run turtle-release programs to help hatchlings survive and to educate visitors about the importance of protecting wildlife in Bali.
14. Deer (Menjangan Island)
West forests are home to barking deer, a type of muntjac from the Muntiacus family, which is part of the broader Cervidae deer family. These shy Bali native animals are primarily found in West Bali National Park and on Menjangan Island, a pristine islet that has retained much of its untouched natural beauty.
The word Menjangan itself is an old local term meaning “deer.” In the past, these deer had natural predators, the Bali tiger. However, if you are wondering if there are tigers on this island, the answer is no: the Bali tiger was declared extinct in 2008 due to poaching and habitat loss.
Sadly, the Menjangan deer are also endangered, as they are often hunted illegally for their antlers. Conservation efforts are ongoing to protect these important wild animals in Bali.
As one of the world’s biggest dive sites, it is world-famous for manta rays (Mobula alfredi). These giant rays, with wingspans up to 4 meters, are often seen around Nusa Penida and Manta Point. Divers and snorkelers frequently encounter these gentle giants gliding gracefully along reef ledges, making them one of the most spectacular marine Bali animals to witness.
The large ocean sunfish, or mola mola, is another fascinating creature often spotted near deep-water currents. They typically reside near the coral reefs of Nusa Penida.
However, travelers should be aware that the currents around Nusa Penida can be dangerous during certain weather conditions, so caution and guidance from local dive operators are essential.
Bali has both large fruit bats and smaller insect-eating bats. They usually live in caves such as Goa Lawah (translated as “bat’s cave”) or in banana leaf buds. Flying foxes, which are big fruit bats, roost in forests like Bali Barat National Park.
At dusk, you may see bats flying out to eat fruit or drink nectar. These animals play an important role in pollinating trees and dispersing seeds, making them a vital part of wildlife in Bali.
This island also is home to several species of frogs, such as Microhyla orientalis (known as Percil Bali) and Polypedates leucomystax. According to a Mongabay report in 2013, the smallest frog in here was discovered, about the size of a human fingernail, also belonging to the Percil family.
Many frogs and toads live in ponds and rice fields. You’ll hear frogs croaking loudly after rain in the wet season. These animals in Bali help control insects and are harmless to humans.
Balinese people believe that frog sounds are a sign that the rainy season in Bali has started or that blessings are on their way, giving frogs a symbolic place among native animals.
18. Luwak (Asian Palm Civet)
The Indonesian word luwak refers to the Asian palm civet, a nocturnal mammal found in jungles. This cat-like animal eats fruit (including coffee cherries) at night and can be found in several regions such as Tegallalang, Tabanan, Karangasem, and Jembrana.
Luwaks are famous for producing kopi luwak (civet coffee) from beans they excrete, creating a complex taste that is soft, sweet, with hints of chocolate and fruit. Luwaks generally avoid people, so you are unlikely to see one in daylight.
Even though they may look similar to possums or sloths, they actually belong to the Viverridae family, relatives of the bearcat. This makes them unique among wild animals in Bali.
Animals in Bali That Have Strong Sound
Some animals in Bali can be very loud, producing strong sounds that may disturb light sleepers. Here are the animals known for their distinctive calls:
Roosters crow at dawn and continue throughout the day. The familiar “cock-a-doodle-doo” is one of the island’s most common sounds. Early risers on this island are used to the lively chorus of roosters greeting the morning.
The Tokay gecko, a large household lizard, makes a loud “tok-kay” call at night. If you stay in a villa, you may hear these chirps echoing from the walls after dark. While startling at first, geckos are harmless insect-eaters that help reduce mosquitoes. If the sound bothers you, villa staff can safely catch and remove them.
Stray cats may meow or yowl, especially when mating season. Their calls are not as booming as a rooster’s crow, but in quiet rural areas you may hear neighborhood cats communicating at night. Compared to other wild animals in Bali, cats are far less noisy.
Some birds on this island are highly vocal. Morning time here often begins with a chorus of birdsong, especially in Ubud or West Bali. Flocks of parrots and bulbuls can screech or chatter loudly, and the starling has a distinctive call. Even doves, with their soft cooing, add to the soundtrack of wildlife in Bali.
Tips for Facing Animals in Bali
Even though most of Bali’s animals are not dangerous, you should still pay attention to your safety. Here are some tips for facing animals in this tropical paradise.
1. Keep your distance
Never approach or attempt to pet wild or stray animals such as monkeys, dogs, or cats. Even those that seem friendly can bite or carry diseases like rabies. Respect their space and do not feed them.
2. Protect yourself at night
Wear shoes and long clothing when walking in rural areas. Keep doors and windows closed or screened after dark to avoid insects and snakes. Always check bedding or shoes for small creatures like geckos, spiders, or centipedes when staying in rustic villas.
Use mosquito repellent daily, especially at dawn and dusk. Mosquitoes in Bali can carry dengue fever and, rarely, malaria. Sleep under nets or use coils if outdoors in the evening, and avoid standing water where mosquitoes breed.
4. Embrace helpful critters
Not all unexpected animals in Bali are dangerous. Geckos inside your room, for instance, feed on mosquitoes and ants. Instead of killing them, allow these insect-eating lizards to roam, they help keep bugs away.
Guidelines for Interacting with Animals in Bali
Visitors should still act responsibly. Always supervise children near monkeys or dogs, and never chase or handle wild animals in Bali.
If you are still concerned about encounters with animals, remember that most of Bali’s resorts and guides prioritize guest safety. For example, Ini Vie Hospitality, one of Bali’s leading hotel operators, ensures that all its properties are carefully managed and supervised to keep guests safe from harmful creatures and to maintain the balance between comfort and wildlife in Bali.

title: Bali Culture Explained: Traditions, Religion & Daily Life
content:
Bali’s culture is often the quiet detail that goes unnoticed in conversations about the island. For most people, beautiful beaches, vibrant nightlife, and the idea of a holiday escape are the main things they focus on and remember.
Bali is not just a tourist destination, but a place where Hindu tradition, art, and communities have grown for thousands of years, shaping the island’s beauty and history. If you want to understand Bali culture better, this article invites you to explore its traditions, beliefs, and daily life.
The Foundation: Tri Hita Karana
When talking about Bali culture, it is important to start from the basics. Tri Hita Karana is the core philosophy that guides how Balinese people live their lives, and it comes from Balinese Hinduism, meaning “three causes of well-being.”
This philosophy teaches the importance of harmony in three key relationships: humans with God (Parahyangan), humans with others (Pawongan), and humans with nature (Palemahan). These values are deeply rooted in Balinese culture and traditions.
Even though it originates in Bali, the values of Tri Hita Karana of Bali are universal and can be applied anywhere. Here is a clearer explanation of each principle.
Parahyangan: Harmony Between Humans and God
Parahyangan comes from the words “Pra,” meaning noble, and “Hyang,” meaning God and all His manifestations. It teaches people to build a harmonious relationship with God through religious practices such as ceremonies (yadnya), prayer, and respect for sacred places.
This relationship is expressed through daily rituals and devotion. Offerings like canang sari in Bali are a simple way to show gratitude and maintain spiritual balance in daily life culture.
Pawongan: Harmony Among People
Pawongan comes from the word “Wong,” which means human. It focuses on building good and respectful relationships among people.
This can be seen in daily life, where people follow social values, ethics, and cooperation within the banjar community in Bali. As a result, relationships remain stable, peaceful, and harmonious.
Palemahan: Harmony with Nature
Palemahan comes from the word “Lemah,” meaning land or environment. It teaches people to maintain a balanced and respectful relationship with nature.
In daily life, this includes caring for the environment, protecting nature, and avoiding actions that damage it. Here, nature is considered an important part of life that must always be respected.
Tri Hita Karana in Daily Life and Architecture
As a life philosophy, Tri Hita Karana is deeply rooted in daily activities, traditions, and art. It also helps Bali preserve its cultural diversity despite the growing influence of globalization.
This philosophy is clearly seen in Balinese architecture, where buildings are designed to create harmony between humans, nature, and God. Both traditional and modern structures follow this principle.
In architecture, Parahyangan is shown through the presence of a family temple (sanggah or pamerajan), usually located in the northeast (kaja-kangin) area of the house. This is considered the most sacred part of a Balinese home.
Pawongan can be seen in layouts that support social interaction, such as the central courtyard (natah) or shared spaces like the banjar. These areas are used for gathering and strengthening community relationships.
Palemahan is reflected in the use of natural materials such as wood, bamboo, and stone. Buildings are also designed to follow the natural shape of the land, showing respect for the environment.
By applying Tri Hita Karana in architecture, buildings on this island are not only functional but also spiritual and environmentally conscious. This is what makes the Bali culture unique and meaningful.
Religion: Balinese Hinduism
Another important part of Bali culture is its religion. The Balinese people follow Hinduism, which shares the same roots as Hinduism in India but has developed in its own unique way.
This difference often comes from local history and cultural influences. As a result, Balinese culture and traditions combine Hindu teachings with animism and ancestor worship.
In Bali, people believe that spirits exist in nature and that ancestors remain present in daily life. This is why rituals and offerings, such as the canang sari, are prepared and presented daily as a sign of gratitude and balance.
Temples, or pura, are also central in Bali’s Hinduism. Each family, village, and region has its own temple, and ceremonies are held regularly based on the traditional calendar, which shapes many of Bali’s ceremonies and festivals.
Another unique feature is the concept of direction, especially kaja and kelod. Kaja refers to the mountains and is considered sacred, while kelod refers to the sea and represents the more worldly side of life.
This system influences how homes, temples, and villages are built. It shows how Balinese daily life culture is closely connected to spiritual beliefs.
The Role of Community: Banjar System
Life in Bali is well organized, and one of the key systems that supports this is the banjar system. A banjar is a local administrative and social unit that helps manage village life and plays an important role in shaping Bali culture.
Similar to a neighborhood association, a banjar is a community with clear boundaries and responsibilities. It has the authority to manage local affairs based on traditions, customs, and social values that are respected within the Indonesian system.
Historically, the Balinese banjar system was first used to manage irrigation for rice fields. As time went on, its role expanded to include broader responsibilities such as handling administrative matters, including identity documents for locals and temporary permits for newcomers, as well as organizing Bali ceremonies and festivals.
The banjar system also shows how Balinese daily life culture is strongly based on community rather than individual interests. People are expected to participate, contribute, and support one another in both daily activities and important events.
More than just an administrative system, the banjar acts as a center for cultural, religious, and social life. It becomes a place where Balinese culture and traditions are preserved, practiced, and passed down through generations.
Through the banjar, cooperation and togetherness are maintained within the community. This is why Balinese society remains closely connected, with strong values of unity, mutual help, and shared responsibility.
Major Ceremonies & Festivals in Bali Culture
As an island with strong traditions rooted in Hindu beliefs, Balinese culture is rich with ceremonies and rituals throughout the year. These ceremonies and festivals are deeply woven into daily life and are part of what makes the island so unique and meaningful.
When visiting, you will often witness traditions that are still actively practiced by the local community. Here are some of the main festivals and important celebrations in Bali:
1. Nyepi (Day of Silence)
Nyepi Bali marks the Balinese New Year and usually takes place around March. On this day, the entire island comes to a complete stop, with no travel, no work, no lights, and no noise, allowing time for reflection, fasting, and meditation.
Melasti is a purification ritual held a few days before Nyepi. It aims to cleanse both the human soul (buana alit) and the universe (buana agung), and is usually performed at the sea or in lakes using holy water (tirta amerta).
Bali’s Ogoh-Ogoh parade takes place on the night before Nyepi, known as Pengrupukan. Large demon statues representing Bhuta Kala (negative forces) are carried through the streets and symbolically removed to purify the environment.
4. Galungan & Kuningan
Galungan Kuningan Bali is celebrated every 210 days over a period of 10 days. It marks the victory of Dharma (good) over Adharma (evil), with streets decorated by penjor, followed by Kuningan as a day to pray for safety and blessings.
Beyond these major celebrations, many other rituals take place regularly throughout the year. All of them follow the traditional Pawukon calendar, a 210-day cycle that keeps spiritual life closely connected to daily routines in Bali’s culture.
Balinese Traditional Arts & Performance
Not only is Bali’s culture rich in ceremonies, but it is also known for its captivating traditional arts and performances. Experiencing these performances is an essential part of any visit to Bali.
Watching traditional performances is one of the most memorable things to do in Bali. Here are some of the most popular and meaningful art forms rooted in local culture:
Kecak dance in Bali is one of the most iconic performances. It is unique because it does not use musical instruments, but instead relies on the rhythmic chanting of “cak-cak-cak” by a circle of male performers.
The dance tells the story of the Ramayana, especially the kidnapping of Sinta. It is commonly performed every day at 6:00 PM at Uluwatu Temple, where you can also enjoy a stunning sunset view.
The Legong dance in Ubud is a classical performance known for its graceful and complex movements. It was once performed only for royal families, but today it can be enjoyed by everyone.
You can watch this dance at Ubud Palace at 7:30 PM every evening. The performance reflects elegance, discipline, and the richness of traditional storytelling.
Gamelan is a traditional music ensemble that plays an important role in performances and ceremonies. It consists of instruments such as metallophones, drums, and gongs, creating a layered and rhythmic sound.
You can experience gamelan performances in cultural centers, temples, and during ceremonies, often in the evening. It is an essential part of Bali daily life culture and often accompanies dance and rituals.
4. Wayang Kulit (Shadow Puppetry)
Wayang kulit is a traditional shadow puppet performance that has been preserved for generations. A puppeteer, known as a dalang, tells stories using leather puppets behind a white screen, accompanied by gamelan music.
This performance is usually held at Oka Kartini every Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday at 8:00 PM. It often shares moral and spiritual lessons from ancient epics.
5. Bali Arts Festival
The Bali Arts Festival is the largest cultural event on the island. It usually takes place from June to July at Taman Werdhi Budaya Art Center, featuring a wide range of performances from morning until evening, including dance, music, and art exhibitions.
Beyond these, there are many other performances such as the Barong dance and local village shows. These art forms remain a strong attraction and an important expression of the Bali culture.
How to Experience Bali Culture Authentically
To truly experience the authenticity of Bali culture, you can start with simple things during your visit. Try connecting with locals by visiting small warungs or neighborhood shops, and explore Balinese souvenirs such as handicrafts, snacks, or traditional products to bring home a meaningful memory.
You can also learn more about Balinese culture and traditions by joining activities like a canang sari workshop or watching traditional performances such as Kecak Dance in Uluwatu, Legong Dance in Ubud, and others. These experiences help you understand the deeper meaning behind local art and rituals.
Another way is to visit local villages, especially during ceremonies, where you can see traditions in their most authentic form. You can also enjoy slower moments, such as experiencing a Balinese spa and massage or having dinner at family-run eateries, where you can taste authentic local flavors in a warm and intimate setting.
In the end, Bali is not only about its natural beauty, but also its rich cultural heritage. Understanding Bali culture as a tourist will make the journey more meaningful and leave a lasting impression beyond the trip itself.
1. What religion do Balinese people practice?
The majority of Balinese people practice Hinduism, specifically Balinese Hinduism, which combines Hindu teachings with local traditions and spiritual beliefs. Religion plays an important role in daily life in Bali, influencing ceremonies, temple rituals, traditional arts, and community activities.
2. What are the main festivals in Bali?
Some of the main festivals celebrated in Bali include Nyepi (Day of Silence), Melasti, the Ogoh-Ogoh Parade, Galungan, and Kuningan. These festivals are deeply connected to Balinese Hindu traditions and are often marked by ceremonies, temple offerings, cultural performances, and community gatherings across the island.
3. Is it disrespectful to visit temples in Bali?
Visiting temples in Bali is completely welcome and is a common part of many travelers’ experiences on the island. However, it becomes disrespectful when visitors ignore local customs, dress inappropriately, enter restricted sacred areas, or fail to follow temple etiquette and regulations.
Nyepi marks the Balinese New Year and usually takes place around March each year. During Nyepi, the entire island comes to a complete stop with no travel, no work, minimal lights, and limited noise, creating a day dedicated to reflection, fasting, meditation, and spiritual cleansing.
Final Thought on Bali Culture
Bali is more than just a beautiful island with stunning tourist attractions. Behind its beaches, mountains, and tropical scenery, Bali has a rich culture shaped by deep traditions, spirituality, history, and a unique way of life that makes the island truly special.
When visiting Bali, it is important to travel with respect and awareness to help preserve the island’s beauty, not only in its nature and beaches, but also in its communities, beliefs, traditions, and cultural heritage. The more you understand Bali culture, the more meaningful and memorable your experience on the island will become.

title: Bali in August: What to Expect, Events & Best Places to Stay
content:
Have you ever wondered, “What is Bali in August?” There is a special moment that you will experience when visiting Bali. You can expect warmer weather, less rainfall, and sunny, clear blue skies when visiting the island in that month.
As August has become one of the best months to visit for an enjoyable trip, you can plan to visit Bali in that month. So, discover Bali in August to know what to expect, what events to attend, and the best places to stay.
Bali Weather in August
When visiting Bali in August, you can expect to have:
Average daytime temperatures: 27°C to 30°C (81°F–86°F).
Evening and early morning temperatures: 22°C to 24°C (72°F–75°F).
Humidity: It is lower than in the wet season, creating more comfortable conditions.
Rainfall: Rarely happens, with only a few rainy days throughout the month.
Sunshine: Sunny with clear blue skies, as the sun shines 8- 10 hours per day.
This Bali weather in August is not so different from Bali in June. It supports you doing outdoor activities, enhancing your trip as you can explore all sides of Bali. It is less worrying since rain rarely happens.
Besides the weather, many things make August unique in Bali. You will experience several events that enrich your trip on Dewata Island, so you will bring new core memories once you leave the island.
What Makes August Unique in Bali
1. Hari Kemerdekaan Indonesia – 17 Agustus
August is a special month for locals in Bali, as the island is located in Indonesia. You will see the citizens celebrate Hari Kemerdekaan Indonesia, also known as Indonesian Independence Day, on 17 August.
In celebrating Hari Kemerdekaan Indonesia, locals still preserve the Tri Hita Karana. It shows how locals respect their heritage, as it connects them with God, people, and nature for prosperity and well-being.
There will be numerous races and competitions in Bali during Independence Day, so you can even take part in local events. Tug of war, rice sack races (lomba balap karung), and many other activities are demonstrated at the event, which is often conducted in an open area.
Besides Hari Kemerdekaan Indonesia, August is Bali’s high season, when they hold a kite festival. These events make Bali a honeymoon destination because you can explore many things with your partner and blend in with locals.
2. Bali Kites Festival
Bali Kites Festival is held in August. Historically, the festival was a seasonal religious event to thank Hindu gods for an abundant harvest. Today, it has evolved into fierce, friendly community competitions to showcase their handcrafted kites.
You will, at least, find three types of kites that are being flown during the Bali dry season in August, which are:
Bebean: A fish-shaped kite that looks like a split-tailed fish.
Janggan: A bird-shaped kite with an amazing, flowing fabric tail that can stretch for over 100 meters.
Pecukan: A leaf-shaped kite with unstable flight that requires the highest level of skill to fly without crashing.
These kites have a unique sound when being flown. You will hear a low, humming vibration in the air. It comes from the guwang (bow) attached to the kites, as the wind passes through and the sound tingles your ears.
There is another event to attend in addition to these two. The Post-Arts Festival Cultural Scene takes place in Ubud in August.
3. Post-Arts Festival Cultural Scene (Ubud)
In August, you can experience the post-arts festival cultural scene, such as Ubud Villa Jazz. Included in a Bali August travel guide, the trip will be more spectacular because you can see the authentic side of Balinese arts and traditions.
You will see traditional dance performances at Ubud’s temples or cultural venues almost every evening. Local art galleries and museums feature rotating exhibitions by Balinese and international artists.
In addition, you can enjoy cultural workshops such as Balinese cooking classes, batik making, gamelan lessons, and traditional dance classes. These are available, so you can choose one activity that fits your preferences.
All these events make Bali a romantic honeymoon destination in Indonesia. You and your partner can do things to do in Bali, beginning with the natural world, its culture, and local heritage-preserving events.
Things to Do in Bali in August
You can explore Bali with things to do. It offers you a stretch of nature. You should choose a location to visit and include it in your itinerary because each side of the island has its own specialties.
1. Snorkeling & Diving
If you want to go snorkeling & diving, you can visit west Bali holiday destinations, like Pulau Menjangan. In this area, you will see the beauty of reefs and marine life. Exploring seasonal marine life such as manta rays and mola mola is possible here.

title: Bali in December: Weather, Travel Tips, and Things to Do
content:
The end of the year is a popular time for a holiday, and December is clearly a good time to visit Bali due to its charming environment, cheap price, and less crowded since Bali in December falls in the wet season. Despite the rain, December is still a vibrant and festive month on the island, full of unique experiences with the warm spirit of Christmas and New Year.
This article aims to provide comprehensive information about visiting this island in December, covering the typical weather conditions and essential travel tips for maximizing your fun. Here is your complete guide to weather in Bali in December, travel tips, and things to do.
Bali Weather in December
As part of Indonesia’s tropical climate, this island is defined by high humidity and frequent rainfall especially in December. Weather here can include heavy but short showers, usually in the afternoon or overnight.
While it rains more often, you can still enjoy hours of sunshine daily, with temperatures consistently between 27°C and 32°C. Compared to winter in other countries, Bali in December is warm, humid, and lush.
Essential Travel Tips for Bali in December
Traveling to Bali in December requires a slightly different approach than visiting during the dry season to ensure maximum comfort. Here are the essential things that you should bring during the Bali rainy season.
1. Pack smart for wet weather
Bring lightweight, fast-drying clothes along with a compact rain jacket or poncho to handle sudden showers. Bring some medicine to avoid fever because of the weather shift or Bali Belly.
2. Expect heavier traffic
Roads become busier as Christmas and New Year approach, so plan extra travel time between destinations.
3. Consider seasonal pricing
Early December is generally more affordable, but prices increase sharply from the week before Christmas until New Year.
4. Book early for peak season
To secure good rates and availability, make your flight and accommodation reservations well in advance.
Things to Do in Bali in December
Despite the occasional rain, there is a wealth of fantastic activities and attractions to enjoy when visiting Bali in December.
The rivers are full and fast during the rainy season, making December an ideal time for exciting water activities. The most recommended place to experience white-water rafting is Ayung River, which offers a thrilling adventure through the jungle, becoming even more lush after the rains.
This river is also quite safe during the rainy season, with no excessive water volume or flooding. You can also find many local warungs or restaurants that are a must-visit after rafting and stay in the villa nearby, which gives you a convenient location before and after rafting.
December is perfect for focusing on indoor wellness, and this tropical island is globally famous for its incredible yoga studios. You can experience a tranquil yet relaxing yoga session across Bali’s popular destinations like Ubud, Sanur, Seminyak, Uluwatu, or Canggu.
After a yoga session, you can also enjoy a nutritious and delicious meal in the café nearby. Taking a relaxing or challenging class is a wonderful way to spend a rainy morning or evening with the island’s charm.
The wellness environment in Islands of God is well-established, with numerous spa brands offering a wide array of treatments to help you unwind. Rainy days are best enjoyed indoors, and there is no better indoor luxury than a spa treatment or massage in Bali.
You can choose the right spa outlet that fits your budget. Affordable spas typically cost around IDR150,000–IDR200,000; mid-scale spas range from IDR250,000–IDR500,000; and luxury spas can be more than IDR500,000.
Padel and tennis have become increasingly popular workouts in Indonesia over the last two years, including in Bali, where many courts are being built across the island. This allows you to stay active and dry, providing great indoor kids’ activities for older children as well.
Many resorts and clubs in areas like Canggu and Seminyak offer high-quality, covered tennis or padel courts. If your hotel or resort does not provide any tennis or padel facilities, you can visit rented courts nearby.
For families traveling with children, you do not need to worry about your kids becoming bored, because it has numerous children’s play venues that offer complete facilities and a safe environment for family holidays in Bali.
Kids and parents can enjoy the relaxing yet playful atmosphere of the many indoor playgrounds located around the tourist hubs. These provide a fun and educational way to burn off energy when the beach is too wet.
Bali offers a world-class dining experience with numerous trendy cafés, calming eateries, and fine-dining restaurants. The best time to experience the culinary journey here is December, where you can stay inside, enjoy a warm meal, and admire the island’s lush environment.
You can expect to spend around IDR100,000 per person for a basic meal, and this can increase depending on the venue.
7. Staycation at A Resort with Complete Facilities
A staycation at beautiful resorts is one of the best ways to enjoy the December holiday on this island. Booking a stay at a resort or villa with a private pool and complete facilities is a smart way to ensure comfort during the rainy season.
When the rain hits, you can enjoy a private swim, relax with in-villa dining, or watch Netflix in comfort. Some resorts also offer fun things to do such as art and craft classes, yoga sessions, spa treatments, and gyms to help you stay active during your holiday.
8. Celebrate Holiday in Bali: Christmas and New Year’s
Even though this island has a predominantly Hindu population, Christmas in Bali is widely celebrated. Christmas in Bali is marked by special dinners, festive decorations, and holiday events hosted by many hotels and restaurants.
Beyond Christmas, New Year’s Eve in Bali is spectacular, often featuring beachside fireworks displays and extravagant celebrations that create a memorable ending to your trip. Do not forget to check some of the island’s popular venues, from restaurants and cafés to beach clubs, that host Christmas events in December.
Bali in December? There’s nothing to fear, only to enjoy
While you should expect some rainfall, Bali in December is a vibrant and exciting time to visit. The December weather creates a unique atmosphere where the rice paddies are at their greenest, and the island is filled with holiday energy. If you bring proper rain gear and plan your activities ahead of time, you will enjoy a truly memorable trip.

title: Bali in January: A Complete Travel Guide and Practical Advice
content:
Are you ready to explore Bali in January? The weather will be warmer and greener, with occasional tropical rain showers. Indonesia has two main seasons: dry (April to October) and rainy (October to April). So, in January, the weather falls within the rainy season, but that doesn’t mean you can’t have an amazing vacation.
This article offers information and guidance for vacationing in Bali during January, complete with a practical travel guide and helpful tips.
Is January a Good Time to Visit Bali?
Absolutely! January brings Bali’s lush, green beauty to life, though it’s also the heart of the monsoon season. Don’t worry, rain on the island usually comes in short, heavy bursts and rarely lasts all day. You’ll still feel the warm, tropical humidity that makes Bali feel so alive.
Thanks to the rain, places like Ubud and the highlands become incredibly fresh and vibrant. Plus, with fewer visitors around, you can enjoy a quieter, more relaxed atmosphere. Just keep in mind that temperatures in January stay warm, but the west monsoon can stir up stronger waves along the west coast, making eastern beaches like Sanur or Candidasa calmer and clearer.
If you don’t mind a passing shower and love the idea of a more peaceful, budget-friendly escape, January is a wonderful time to experience Bali’s natural charm without the crowds.
Best area to stay in Bali in January
When planning where to stay in Bali in January, it’s important to consider the weather. Here are some tips for choosing the best areas to stay during this time.
Ubud in January is a magical and romantic choice. The tropical rain only adds to the charm of this cultural haven, making the lush rice paddies even greener and more vibrant.
This month is perfect for wellness tourism, with many activities focused on relaxation and rejuvenation, or simply relaxing at one of the top resorts and spas in the area.
For those seeking a close connection to nature, Equipoise Resort, with its rice paddy views, or Aksari Resort, nestled among the forests, offer the perfect retreats. If you’re wondering about Bali weather in January, Ubud’s cozy atmosphere makes it ideal yoga, meditation, and spa treatments.
If you’re hoping for some beach time in January, Sanur is a great choice. Located on Bali’s east coast, it’s more sheltered from the rainy season winds than the west coast, which makes the beaches here calmer and the water cleaner.
The area offers a peaceful stay, perfect for those seeking a quieter vibe. Seascape Resort and Sanora Villa are excellent options, combining tranquility with easy access to local attractions.
With less traffic and a more laid-back atmosphere, it’s definitely a good time to go to Bali if you want a relaxing getaway near the ocean.
3. Seminyak & Canggu
For those looking for a livelier scene in January, Seminyak and Canggu are the places to be. These areas are buzzing with cafes, fine dining restaurants, and boutique shopping, and even when it rains. There are plenty of aesthetic indoor spots for what to do in Seminyak and Canggu.
While the beaches here may not be in their best condition during the rainy season, the vibrant energy more than makes up for it. If you’re looking for accommodations close to everything, Sini Vie Resort in Seminyak is ideal for couples, while Canggu Cabana is perfect for those who want to be near the beach.
At the southern tip of Bali, Uluwatu enjoys slightly less rainfall than central Bali in January. When the rain clears, you’ll be treated to breathtaking views of the cliffs and the ocean, making it the perfect spot for watching sunsets or fireworks
For a stay in this area, consider Seascape Uluwatu, located on a hilltop with stunning views. Alternatively, if you’re after something more private, The Arden Villa offers a secluded escape.
While Kuta might be tempting with its central location, it’s less ideal because the area is heavily affected by westerly winds, which often bring debris to the shore. The area can be crowded, especially when it rains, making it a less comfortable option for relaxation.
However, Kuta offers plenty of affordable accommodation options if you’re looking for budget-friendly stays. Despite the weather, Kuta is still one of the things to do in Bali in January for those seeking a bustling atmosphere and lots of activity.
Things to Do in Bali in January
1. Ubud Day Tour & Rice Paddies
Thanks to the rainfall, the Tegalalang Rice Terraces are at their most vibrant, offering a stunning view of deep green paddies. It’s best to tour in the morning, as rain usually rolls in during the afternoon.
Make sure to wear non-slip shoes, as the paths can get a little muddy. This is one of the best things to do in Ubud in January, as the rice paddies are even more magical in this season.
The waterfalls in Bali, like Tegenungan and Kanto Lampo, are particularly majestic in January. With the rainy season in full swing, the water flow is strong, and the scenery is dramatic. If there’s heavy rain, the water may turn brown, but the surrounding forest is incredibly beautiful, often shrouded in mist.
For the thrill-seekers, an ATV adventure is even more exciting during the rainy season. The muddy tracks and puddles make the ride much more challenging compared to the dry season, offering a real sense of adventure. Get ready to embrace the mud, as this is a “wet” activity designed for fun, not for staying clean.
4. Spa, Wellness, & Yoga
When the rain starts to fall, a visit to a spa or yoga studio in Ubud is the perfect way to unwind. Enjoy a traditional Balinese massage while listening to the soothing sound of rain outside, or practice yoga in one of Ubud’s semi-open studios, like Yoga Barn or Radiantly Alive, where the fresh, earthy scent fills the air. This is the ideal Plan B for a rainy day in Bali.
If you’re looking for an indoor activity, a cooking class in Bali is both fun and educational. Start by visiting a traditional market in the morning to gather fresh ingredients, then head to an open kitchen to learn how to prepare Balinese dishes. It’s perfect for cloudy and rainy days.
6. Cafe Hopping in Seminyak
Seminyak is home to a variety of beautiful and aesthetic cafes, perfect for a rainy day. January is slightly quieter than December, making it the perfect time to visit spots like Nook, Sisterfields, and Revolver, where you can enjoy delicious food and drinks without the usual long wait. It’s a great way to explore things to do in Seminyak on a relaxing day.
Despite the rain, shopping at Sunday markets in Canggu is still a fun experience. The laid-back atmosphere means you can shop around comfortably, and you might even score some bargains during the low season. If you’re looking for things to do in Canggu with kids, visiting the market can be an enjoyable family activity.
Exploring Bali’s temples, like Tirta Empul or Ulun Danu Beratan, is a truly spiritual experience in January. The cooler, misty weather adds a mystical touch to the atmosphere, making it perfect for photography
Workshops such as silver making or knitting are perfect alternatives in January because they are conducted entirely indoors, so your plans won’t be disrupted by rain. These activities are very popular in Canggu and Ubud, providing a peaceful, creative experience while waiting for the weather to clear up.
In addition to taking home your own creations, these activities are the best choice for things to do in Canggu on a rainy day.
What to wear in Bali in January
When figuring out how to dress for Bali in January, it’s important to keep the rainy season and high humidity in mind. Opt for lightweight, breathable fabrics like cotton, linen, or rayon that will keep you cool and dry quickly if you get caught in a downpour.
Be sure to pack a raincoat and a small umbrella, especially if you’ll be spending time outdoors or traveling. Practical footwear, like hiking sandals or flip-flops, is a must, something that can handle wet conditions without getting ruined. This way, you’ll stay comfortable and prepared no matter the weather.
Final Thought on Bali in January
Bali in January offers a unique blend of lush landscapes, cultural experiences, and tranquil vibes, making it a great time to explore the island despite the rain. From adventure to relaxation, this season provides a refreshing Bali experience away from the crowds.
For added comfort during your stay, consider booking a boutique hotel from Ini Vie Hospitality, offering personalized services and cozy accommodations perfect for Bali in January. With a focus on comfort and style, it’s the ideal place to unwind after a day of exploring.
